newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters-UPS deal a boost to U.S. labor - analysts. [CORRECTED 23:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Teamsters-UPS deal a boost to U.S. labor - analysts. [CORRECTED 23:45 GMT]

text.p: The Teamsters union's success in waging the nation's biggest strike in two decades gives the fragile labor movement a shot in the arm and may mark the start of a new era of union strength, labor experts said Tuesday.

Although the circumstances that allowed the union to win a settlement with United Parcel Service are unique, the fact that the high-profile strike did not end in disaster for labor was in itself a victory, labor scholars and historians said.
"It offers the hope of victory, which had been missing," said Alan Draper, a professor of government at St. Lawrence University in Canton, N.Y., who has written about labor.

In the years since President Ronald Reagan fired thousands of members of the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (PATCO) during an illegal strike in 1981, organized labor often watched helplessly in other disputes as union members were permanently replaced by companies.

"This is the end of the PATCO syndrome," said University of Virginia historian Nelson Lichtenstein, whose writings on the labor movement include a biography of labor leader Walter Reuther entitled, "The Most Dangerous Man in Detroit."
"1981 was the beginning of a dramatic era of decline in union strength and a decline in wage equality," he said. "This strike, I'm sure, will be the reversal of it."

Partly because of PATCO, the strike was deemed all but a useless weapon for American workers, and the number of major work stoppages fell from about 300 a year in the decades after World War II to a low of 31 in 1995 and 37 last year.

The Teamsters strike was different, experts said. The union, whose strike fund was largely depleted, got support from the AFL-CIO, the 78-union labor federation, which cobbled together $10 million to pay $55 a week in benefits to the 185,000 strikers at UPS.
It was a rare display of solidarity for the American labor movement but one typical of the aggressive new administration of AFL-CIO President John Sweeney, experts said.

The 15-day UPS strike, the largest in more than 20 years, was also unusual since Americans sided heavily with the strikers despite the inconvenience the walkout caused, polls showed. This underscored that many workers are worried about stagnant wages and their jobs, the experts said.

The UPS settlement shows unions can still wage old-fashioned strikes and win, though UPS has been considered generally union-friendly and operates in a service business where jobs cannot be exported, they said. It would have had trouble hiring replacements in the current tight labor market.
But other experts said the settlement would do little more than energize union activists and give them hope that unions could still fight such battles and win.

"The kind of agreement that you see here is not going to be easy to replicate in other industries where there are part-time workers and where management can up the ante more than UPS could," Draper (corrects attribution from Lichtenstein) said.

Under the deal reached late Monday, UPS agreed to Teamster proposals to convert 10,000 part-time jobs into higher paying full-time jobs, to phase out most subcontracting and to narrow the pay gap between full- and part-time workers.
In touting the settlement, International Brotherhood of Teamsters President Ron Carey said it would usher in a new era for the beleaguered labor movement.
"American workers have shown that we (can) stand up to corporate greed," he said. "This victory shows that American workers are on the move again.

That view was sharply disuputed by Peter Eide, manager of labor law policy at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, who called the settlement even-handed and noted that UPS has long had cordial relations with the Teamsters union.

"I don't think that anybody can say that this was a victory for organized labor," he said. "They've had a long, long relationship with the Teamsters. All of the people in this organization used to be Teamsters."
One sign of whether the strike has a lasting impact, labor scholars said, will be if it helps union organizers show non-union workers the labor movement has something to offer, and can deliver.

Union membership has been dropping for decades, falling to 16.3 million last year, only 14.5 percent of all wage and salaried employees, from about a third of all workers in the 1950s. The recent percentage is among the lowest in industrialized nations.
